passage: After news of a riot in a city far away, Farhana stopped waiting at the bus stop. Farhana, who shared her Eid sewaiyan with Rashmi every year, now answered messages with one word. In their small town near Nashik, Rashmi, fifteen, felt a cold knot in her stomach. Jatin from class whispered that Farhana's family had warned her to stay away. Rashmi did not want to believe it. On Saturday she carried a packet of pakoras to Farhana's house. Farhana's mother let her in, and Farhana stared at the floor. "Have I done something?" Rashmi asked. "No," Farhana said finally. "Ammi is scared people will blame us for what strangers did." Rashmi shook her head. "I don't blame you for anything you didn't do. You're my friend." They ate the pakoras on the roof. On Monday Farhana was at the bus stop.

qa.q: What did Rashmi bring to Farhana's house?
qa.a: Rashmi brought a packet of pakoras.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when Farhana stopped answering properly?
qa.a: Rashmi felt worried and hurt, with a cold knot in her stomach, but she did not want to believe the rumour.

qa.q: Which choice by Rashmi kept the friendship alive?
qa.a: Rashmi went to Farhana's house, asked honestly whether she had done something, and said she did not blame Farhana for what strangers did.

qa.q: Why had Farhana pulled away?
qa.a: Farhana's mother was scared that people would blame their family for what strangers did, so Farhana stayed away out of fear and shame.

grounding: A teenager finds a friend of another faith pulling away after a news event and keeps trust alive by staying in touch and asking honestly.

passage: Kwame, fifteen, noticed that Ines had started eating lunch in the library. She used to save him a seat in the canteen and swap almond biscuits for his mum's plantain chips. Now she only nodded. Ines's family went to the mosque on Fridays, and Kwame sang in his church choir, and until now it had never mattered. After a week, Kwame texted, "Did I do something?" Ines wrote back, "No. My grandmother says I should stay with my own community after what was said about us on the news." The next day he found her at the tram stop. "I saw the news too," he said. "I don't think you or your family did anything. I'd hate to be blamed for what a stranger did." Ines's shoulders dropped. "I didn't want to bring trouble." "You're not trouble. I miss the biscuits." She laughed, the first time in a week.

qa.q: Where did Kwame find Ines the next day?
qa.a: Kwame found Ines at the tram stop.

qa.q: How might Kwame have felt when Ines began eating lunch in the library?
qa.a: Kwame probably felt puzzled, worried and a bit hurt, which is why he texted to ask whether he had done something.

qa.q: Which choice by Kwame kept the friendship alive?
qa.a: Kwame asked honestly by text, then went to find Ines and said he did not blame her or her family for what a stranger did.

qa.q: Why did Ines pull away?
qa.a: Ines's grandmother told her to stay with her own community after what was said on the news, and Ines did not want to bring trouble to Kwame.

grounding: A teenager finds a friend of another faith pulling away after a family warning and keeps trust alive by asking honestly and refusing to blame the friend.

passage:
Board exams were four days away, and Afreen, sixteen, couldn't concentrate. Her best friend Manjula hadn't replied to a single message since the weekend.
There had been violence in a town two hours away, and it was on every channel. On Monday, Manjula sat at a different desk. On Tuesday, she walked home with other girls.
Afreen's first thought was, She thinks I'm one of "them." Her second was, Maybe her family told her to stay away.
With no time to waste, she wrote a note and slipped it into Manjula's bag: "I miss you. Did something happen? I'm not angry. I just want to know."
On Wednesday, Manjula found her at the gate. Her eyes were red. "My Papa said to keep away for a while. I didn't know how to tell you."
"It's not your fault," Afreen said. "Study with me after the exams? When it's calmer?"
Manjula nodded and squeezed her hand.

qa.q: What did Afreen slip into Manjula's bag?
qa.a: She slipped in a note: "I miss you. Did something happen? I'm not angry. I just want to know."

qa.q: What was Afreen worried about when Manjula pulled away?
qa.a: Afreen was hurt and afraid that Manjula now saw her as one of "them" because of the violence, or had been told to stay away.

qa.q: Why did Afreen's note work better than an angry message?
qa.a: It asked honestly and said she wasn't angry, which made it safe for Manjula to explain instead of hiding.

qa.q: What is it like for Manjula to be told to keep away?
qa.a: Manjula seems torn and sad, with red eyes, caught between her father's warning and her friendship.

grounding: Under exam pressure, a teenager finds a friend of another faith pulling away after violence in the news, and keeps trust by asking honestly and not blaming.

passage:
After the clash in the city made the headlines, Varun Mathew stopped coming to the colony basketball court. Sunaina, seventeen, waited for him three evenings in a row.
She finally knocked at his flat. His mother answered, polite but guarded. Varun came to the door and didn't step out.
"Did I do something?" Sunaina asked.
Varun looked at his feet. "People in our church are scared. My mother thinks we should keep to ourselves for a bit. Your uncle posted something online."
Sunaina's face went hot. She'd seen that post and said nothing.
"That's not what I think," she said. "And you're not responsible for what anyone else did either. I'm sorry I didn't say so sooner."
Varun's shoulders dropped a little. "Court tomorrow?"
"Six o'clock. I'll bring the ball."

qa.q: How many evenings did Sunaina wait at the court?
qa.a: She waited for him three evenings in a row.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when her face went hot?
qa.a: She felt ashamed for having seen her uncle's post and said nothing.

qa.q: What did Sunaina do that kept trust alive?
qa.a: She went to Varun's door, asked honestly, apologised for her silence, and made clear she didn't blame him for others' acts.

qa.q: What is it like for Varun's mother after the clash?
qa.a: She seems guarded and scared, wanting her family to keep to themselves until things feel safer.

grounding: A teenager's friend of another faith pulls away after a news event and a family warning, and she keeps trust by asking honestly and refusing to blame.

passage:
"Rafiq, you've left the cricket group. And you walk home the long way now."
"It's nothing, Jeevan."
"It's been two weeks. Since the thing on the news."
"...Ammi said to be careful. Someone in your street shouted at my cousin."
"My street? Who?"
"Doesn't matter."
"It does. I'm sorry that happened. But I'm still me. We've been friends since Class 2."
"I know. But I got scared you'd think we're all like the men on TV."
"Rafiq. Did you do anything on TV?"
"No!"
"Then why would I blame you? I don't. Not for that, not ever."
"...Okay."
"Walk home with me today, bhai? The short way. I'll walk you to your gate."
"Your mother won't mind?"
"My mother asked where you've been. She misses your chatter."
"Fine. But I'm batting first on Saturday."

qa.q: How long has Rafiq been walking home the long way?
qa.a: It's been two weeks, since the thing on the news.

qa.q: What was Rafiq afraid of?
qa.a: Rafiq was scared that Jeevan would think Rafiq's family were all like the men on TV, and his cousin had been shouted at in Jeevan's street.

qa.q: How did Jeevan help keep the friendship alive?
qa.a: Jeevan asked honestly, apologised for what happened to Rafiq's cousin, said clearly he didn't blame Rafiq, and offered to walk him home.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's mother see Rafiq's absence?
qa.a: She seems to miss Rafiq and to feel no suspicion, asking where he has been.

grounding: A teenager whose friend of another faith pulls away after a news event keeps trust by asking honestly and refusing to blame him for others' acts.

passage: Last March, after the fight near the procession, Yogesh stopped waiting for me at the gate. We had walked to school together since Class 3. His family goes to the temple at the end of our lane; mine goes to the church beside it. For a week he said "busy" and looked at his shoes. I was hurt, and part of me wanted to say something sharp about his people. I didn't. On Saturday I sent him a message: "Did I do something, or is it the stuff in town?" He called that night. His mother had been scared after the fight and had told him to keep his distance for a while. "I'm not scared of you," he said. "I know," I said. "Nobody in our lane threw anything." We walk together again now, a little quieter than before. I'm Sarika, and I learnt that asking beats guessing.

qa.q: Since which class had Sarika and Yogesh walked to school together?
qa.a: They had walked to school together since Class 3.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when Yogesh kept saying "busy"?
qa.a: Sarika felt hurt and confused, and was even tempted to say something sharp about Yogesh's community, but held back.

qa.q: What did Sarika's message get right?
qa.a: It asked honestly and left room for Yogesh to explain, instead of guessing or blaming him for what others did in town.

qa.q: Why might Yogesh have pulled away even though he was not scared of Sarika?
qa.a: His mother was frightened after the fight and told him to keep his distance, so he was caught between her worry and the friendship, which left him awkward and quiet.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager whose friend of another faith pulls away after local trouble and a family warning, and who keeps trust by asking honestly and not blaming the friend.
